name: Sundsvall
title: Sundsvall Thickness Gauging | Pulp, Timber & Container Ships
description: Thickness gauging in Sundsvall for pulp and timber carriers, breakbulk and container ships: cargo hold, tank-top, hatch cover and ice-belt UTM in port.
h1: Hull and Hold Thickness Measurement for Forest Product and Container Ships in Sundsvall
intro: Sundsvall is one of the forest industry's main shipping points on the Bothnian Sea. Pulp, sawn timber and paper from mills in the region leave on breakbulk and container ships, and the new container and breakbulk port at Tunadal, inaugurated in 2024, has opened the bay to larger vessels. Ships loading forest products stay alongside long enough to have holds, tank tops and ballast tanks gauged. A technician team travels from India to the vessel for each job, timed to the confirmed loading window.
keywords: ice class ship gauging bothnian sea

highlights.h: Bigger ships at the Tunadal terminal
highlights.p: SCA's investment in the container and breakbulk port at Tunadal lets larger container and forest product ships call at Sundsvall. Bigger ships bring more holds and larger tank systems, so a gauging scope planned around one loading call needs firm priorities.

Pulp is dense cargo, moved in units by forklifts working inside the hold. Tank tops, hold frames and the lower parts of bulkheads take repeated knocks, so readings and a damage record taken before stowage are valuable evidence for the owner.

highlights.h: Ice season on the Bothnian Sea
highlights.p: The bay off Sundsvall is usually affected by ice for part of the winter, and ships may need ice class and icebreaker help to reach port. The ice belt and bow structure deserve attention in spring, before summer schedules fill up.

port.h: Sundsvall's bay, its terminals and the forest trade
p: Sundsvall stands on the coast of Medelpad, midway up the Swedish side of the Gulf of Bothnia, on a bay sheltered by Alnön, the large island just offshore. Ships reach the port from the open Bothnian Sea along piloted fairways that run past the island, and the terminals lie on the mainland shore, with Tunadal to the north of the city. The bay gives good shelter from the open sea, and the Baltic's absence of tide keeps quayside conditions steady. Winter is the variable: the bay and the coastal waters freeze in most seasons, and in a hard winter ships depend on icebreaker assistance and must meet the traffic restrictions in force for this part of the coast. In summer the same waters are open and calm, and that is when most owners prefer to plan heavier work.

The forest industry built the port and still dominates it. Pulp from SCA's Östrand mill at Timrå, north of the city, sawn timber from sawmills across the region and paper and other forest products are shipped to European and wider markets, together with containers carrying a growing share of the same goods. SCA's investment in Tunadal, completed at the end of 2023 and inaugurated in 2024, created a new container port and cargo-handling areas next to a logistics park with rail connections, built to receive larger container ships and breakbulk vessels. Inbound cargo includes chemicals and raw materials for the region's process industry, and general cargo ships and small bulk carriers serve other local customers. Together, these trades keep a steady flow of short-sea and deep-sea ships coming into the bay through all four seasons.

Ships in the forest trade tend to be purpose-built: open-hatch or box-shaped holds, gantry or deck cranes on some, and strong tank tops designed for heavy unit loads. Their hulls take the ice in winter, their holds take forklift traffic at every loading, and their hatch covers must stay weathertight because paper and pulp are spoiled by water. Container feeders bring the usual feeder concerns of hatch covers, coamings and scrubber piping. A loading at Sundsvall typically takes long enough to work through several holds, and owners who call regularly can spread a larger programme over successive voyages. Exports continue right through the winter, so ice-classed ships call year-round, and the same ship may be seen here in deep ice in February and in open water in July.

facilities.h: Gauging at Tunadal and the other Sundsvall berths
p: Tunadal is where most ships calling at Sundsvall now berth, and it offers room alongside for a team to work around cargo operations. On forest product ships, holds are gauged as the loading plan reaches them, with tank tops, frames and lower bulkheads measured and any cargo-handling damage recorded before the first units go in. Container ships offer shorter windows, suited to hatch covers, coamings, scrubber lines and selected ballast tanks. Smaller quays around the bay serve local industry and are useful for coasters and general cargo ships lying for longer periods.

Sundsvall has no drydock for seagoing ships, so dockings take place at yards elsewhere, around the Baltic or beyond, chosen by the owner and frequently planned for summer when the ice has gone. That makes Sundsvall a natural place for pre-docking gauging: readings taken during a loading show where steel renewal is likely, so the yard specification and the surveyor's close-up plan can be prepared in advance. In winter, work on open decks and the external shell is slowed by frost, wind and short days, while measurements inside holds, tanks and machinery spaces carry on largely unaffected.

Tunadal container berths — hatch covers, coamings, scrubber lines and selected ballast tanks on feeders within the berth window.
Industrial quays around the bay — hold and ballast tank measurements on coasters and general cargo ships serving local industry.
Ships lying idle between cargoes — full condition and pre-purchase gauging over several days.

context.h: Ice-class rules, cargo care and regulation at Sundsvall
p: Ships calling at Sundsvall are inspected under the Paris MoU by the Swedish Transport Agency. In winter the Swedish Maritime Administration sets traffic restrictions for ports along the Bothnian Sea when ice forms, and only ships meeting the minimum ice class and size receive icebreaker assistance. For owners, that turns ice class into a commercial asset for the forest trade, which ships out through the winter. Keeping it means the ice belt and the frames behind it must remain within the margins of the Finnish-Swedish ice-strengthening rules, and wastage or damage found at a spring gauging is usually repaired at the summer docking.

Forest product shippers are demanding customers. Pulp, paper and sawn timber must arrive dry and undamaged, so charterers look closely at hatch covers, coamings, cross-joints and drainage, as well as at holds free of sharp edges and loose scale. Thickness readings on hatch cover plating and coaming structure, together with a record of tank-top and frame condition, give an owner evidence of a well-kept ship when a contract is renewed. Ships under non-EU flags also need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, and the larger ships in this trade now report emissions under the EU ETS.

jobs.p: Forest product ships account for most of the work. Owners and managers use a loading at Sundsvall to gauge holds and tank tops before a survey, to record the hold condition at the start of a charter, or to prepare a steel estimate for the summer docking. Feeders and container ships at Tunadal add short, repeatable scopes on hatch covers and scrubber piping. After a hard winter, ice-classed ships trading here are often given an ice-belt and bow scope, so that any damage can be sized before the yard period. Findings are shared with the superintendent each day, so decisions do not wait for the final report.
list: Tank-top, hold frame and lower bulkhead gauging on a pulp carrier during loading at Tunadal, with forklift damage recorded by frame.
Hatch cover plating and coaming readings on an open-hatch forest product ship ahead of a charter renewal.
Spring ice-belt thickness measurement and MPI at bow frame connections on an ice-classed breakbulk ship.
Scrubber wash-water line and ballast tank gauging on a container ship within its Tunadal berth window.
Pre-docking steel estimate on the double bottom and wing tanks of a timber carrier, ahead of a summer docking.

logistics: Most teams fly into Stockholm Arlanda and continue on a domestic flight to Sundsvall-Timrå Airport, north of the city, or travel north by train along the coast. Technicians come from India on Schengen visas, applied for once the loading date is known with reasonable confidence. Port access at Tunadal and the other terminals is controlled, so the ship's agent registers the team before the call. For winter jobs we plan travel with some margin, because ice can delay arrival and short daylight limits the working day on deck.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while pulp is being loaded at Sundsvall?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the team stays ahead of the cargo. Each hold is measured while it is still empty, so we agree the order with the chief officer and the stevedores and work through the holds in the sequence the loading plan reaches them. Once pulp units are stowed, the tank top and lower frames are covered, so the readings and damage notes for that hold have to be complete by then.

faqs.q: Is the Tunadal terminal suitable for a gauging job on a container ship?
faqs.a: For a targeted scope, yes. Hatch covers, coamings, scrubber piping and accessible deck structure can be measured during cargo operations, and the crew can prepare one or two ballast tanks for entry. The work is planned around crane movements and the berth window. For a ship that calls regularly, larger programmes are divided over several calls.

faqs.q: What does winter mean for a gauging job in Sundsvall?
faqs.a: Mostly a less predictable schedule. Ice can delay arrival while a ship waits for assistance, so we confirm the berth date with the agent before mobilising. Inside the hull the cold has little effect on the work; shell plating and open decks are harder to measure in frost and darkness, so we prefer to place external readings in the open-water season or at the docking.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock near Sundsvall?
faqs.a: Not for seagoing cargo ships, so gauging at Sundsvall is done afloat and full dockings take place at yards elsewhere around the Baltic or further away. Readings taken here are tied to the TM plan's frame and strake references, which lets the docking yard and the class surveyor use them, and our team can travel on to the yard to complete the programme.
